column5: Musa's mother, nursing child, water separation
column6: When Moses' mother can no longer conceal him, she puts him in a waterproof basket among the Nile reeds. It is the concrete biblical water-separation scene beside the commentary's mother who nurses Musa and sends him into the yamm; Exodus supplies concealment as the immediate motive.

column5: Musa's sister watches from afar
column6: Moses' sister stations herself to learn what will happen to him. This is the narrative counterpart to the sister who identifies a household able to foster Musa in the commentary.

column5: mercy for the crying, exposed child
column6: Pharaoh's daughter opens the basket, sees the crying child, and has compassion. Her response makes the commentary's claim that mercy turns toward the weak into the act that begins Moses' rescue.

column5: sister proposes a nursing household
column6: The sister offers to call a Hebrew woman to nurse the child. The same child-sister-household nexus underlies Qur'an 28:12's offer of an ahl bayt who will care for him, though Exodus specifies a wet nurse.

column5: mother is returned as paid nurse
column6: Pharaoh's daughter entrusts the child to his own mother to nurse and pays her. It is the close biblical counterpart to Musa's return to his mother, joining maternal breast, a nonmaternal household, and providential restoration.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter adopts Moses
column6: After he grows, Moses becomes Pharaoh's daughter's son. This makes Qur'an 26:18's collective claim that Pharaoh's household raised Musa a pointedly different household claim: the biblical named foster parent is the daughter, not Pharaoh as speaker.

column5: Moses nurtured in his father's house
column6: Stephen says Moses was brought up for three months in his father's house. The retelling explicitly foregrounds the protected natal home before exposure, which the commentary contrasts with later palace claims.

column5: Pharaoh's daughter raises Moses as son
column6: Acts says that Pharaoh's daughter took up the exposed Moses and raised him as her own son. It preserves the foster-child transition central to the commentary's distinction between birth, nursing, and a later household's nurture.

column5: Moses refuses Egyptian wet nurses
column6: The Bavli expands Exodus 2 by making Moses refuse Egyptian nurses until his own mother feeds him, because his mouth is destined for divine speech. That interpretation intensifies the commentary's claim that his true nurture occurs at his mother's breast under God's care.

column5: source ر ح م: Hebrew רחם/רחמים, nursing mother
column6: The Hebrew r-ḥ-m root supplies the verb for a mother's compassion while the verse speaks of her nursing child and the son of her belly. It is a close Semitic witness to the commentary's womb-to-mercy movement, then extends it to God's unfailing remembrance.

column5: God forms within the mother's womb
column6: The psalm credits God with forming the inward parts and weaving the speaker in the mother's womb. It directly accompanies the commentary's Qur'an 3:6 image of God shaping a person in the rahim as a place of formation.

column5: gestation figured as milk being poured and curdled
column6: Job describes his bodily beginning through liquid and milk-curdling imagery before the later clothing of flesh. Its deliberately domestic, embodied account of gestation belongs beside the commentary's womb as vessel and its lactating-animal image.

column5: God forms and knows the prophet before birth
column6: God says that he formed Jeremiah in the womb and knew him before he came out of it. This gives a biblical instance of prenatal divine formation that develops the commentary's claim that the womb is God's workshop.

column5: God brings the speaker from womb to mother's breasts
column6: The speaker credits God with drawing him from the womb and making him trust at his mother's breasts. It holds together God's hidden guardianship and maternal nourishment, the two agents the commentary distinguishes in Musa's infancy.

column5: God carries people from belly and womb
column6: God addresses those borne from the belly and carried from the womb. The parent-like divine carrying extends the commentary's home-to-maturity image beyond gestation into sustained care.

column5: pain in conception and childbirth
column6: The verse makes painful childbearing part of Eve's condition. It is the direct biblical analogue for the commentary's insistence that the womb-house has a bodily cost after birth, even though its narrative frame is different.

column5: one Maker fashions persons in the womb
column6: Job grounds his refusal to oppress servants in the fact that the same Maker formed both parties in the womb. It turns shared prenatal origin into an ethical relation, illuminating the commentary's move from one womb to kinship and mercy for the vulnerable.

column5: source ر ح م: maternal רחמים acts to save a son
column6: The true mother's compassion, Hebrew rahamim, is stirred for her son and she yields him rather than see him killed. This is not merely emotion: it performs the commentary's definition of rahma as tenderness that entails beneficent action toward the weak.

column5: source ر ح م: fatherly compassion for children
column6: The psalm compares YHWH's compassion for those who fear him to a father's compassion for children, using the r-ḥ-m root. It gives a paternal rendering of the commentary's Rahman/Rahim frame around nurturing lordship.

column5: source ر ح م: divine compassion for a remembered son
column6: Ephraim is called God's dear child; divine inward yearning culminates in the emphatic r-ḥ-m promise of mercy. The verse joins father-son relation and womb-derived compassion, sharpening the commentary's family account of rahma.

column5: Lo-Ruhamah, the child named Not-Compassionated
column6: Hosea's daughter is named Lo-Ruhamah because God announces a withdrawal of r-ḥ-m compassion. Its negative naming makes the repeated Qur'anic merciful names more consequential: mercy can be represented as a relation to a child that is withheld as well as bestowed.

column5: Ruhamah restored by divine mercy
column6: The restoration oracle says that God will show r-ḥ-m compassion to Lo-Ruhamah and restore a belonging relation. Read after Hos. 1:6, it gives a narrative reversal of estrangement into parental mercy relevant to the commentary's merciful enclosing frame.

column5: shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads mothers
column6: The shepherd gathers lambs in his arms, carries them at his breast, and gently leads ewes with young. This joins weak young, maternal animals, and a caregiver's measured pace, supplying a pastoral analogue to the commentary's child and lactating-sheep images.

column5: nurse carries a suckling child
column6: Moses protests that he did not conceive or bear Israel and so cannot carry them as a nurse carries a suckling child. The verse is a precise nonbiological-caregiver analogy for the commentary's rabb/rabba and nurse who undertake a child's nurture.

column5: foster fathers and nursing mothers
column6: Kings are promised as foster fathers and queens as nursing mothers. This explicit pairing of adoptive authority and lactation provides a biblical counterpart to the commentary's nonbirth parent and child-minder senses of the r-b-b family.

column5: Mordecai brings up an orphan as his daughter
column6: Mordecai raises Hadassah after the death of her parents and takes her as his own daughter. It is a concrete household instance of the commentary's claim that raising a child can belong to someone other than the one who gave birth.

column5: Naomi holds the child and becomes his nurse
column6: Naomi takes the newborn to her bosom and becomes his nurse. The scene makes kinship, bodily closeness, and an elder woman's nonmaternal nurture converge in the way the commentary's womb-derived family language invites.

column5: God carries Israel as a parent carries a child
column6: Moses recalls YHWH carrying Israel in the wilderness as a man carries his son. It makes the divine Lord a sustaining parent across a journey, not simply a begetter, matching the commentary's transition from womb to ongoing rabbi-like cultivation.

column5: divine discipline as a father disciplines a son
column6: Israel is to recognize that YHWH disciplines it as a man disciplines his son. This gives a biblical parent-child account of formative correction, a necessary complication and parallel to terbiye as gradual movement toward completion.

column5: children taught by YHWH
column6: All of Zion's children are described as taught by YHWH. The verse directly accompanies the commentary's Rahman who teaches and its extension of rabb into the teacher who feeds learners with small portions of knowledge.

column5: God instructs with an eye upon the learner
column6: God promises to instruct and teach the way to go, counsel the speaker, and keep an eye upon him. It closely matches the commentary's conjunction of teaching and Musa being raised under God's eye.

column5: Abraham directs children and household in God's way
column6: God's election of Abraham is tied to his commanding his children and household after him to keep YHWH's way. It puts religious formation inside the house, as the commentary puts nurture and teaching inside a family setting.

column5: teach the words diligently to children at home
column6: Israel is commanded to teach the words to children while sitting at home, walking, lying down, and rising. This supplies a concrete domestic rhythm for the commentary's claim that upbringing extends into instruction.

column5: Samuel grows in stature and favor
column6: The child Samuel continues to grow in stature and in favor with YHWH and people. It is a concise biblical sequence from protected childhood toward mature, socially and divinely recognized formation.

column5: a household official becomes a father to inhabitants
column6: Eliakim receives office and is called a father to Jerusalem's inhabitants and Judah's house. It translates the commentary's qawwam image of one who upholds a household into public stewardship with explicitly parental language.

column5: food apportioned to the household
column6: The capable woman rises at night to give food to her household and portions to her servants. It realizes the commentary's secondary image of provisions brought into a home as an act that keeps its members alive.

column5: fetus taught Torah in the womb
column6: The Bavli imagines an angel teaching the fetus the whole Torah in the womb before birth. This is an interpretive, not narrative, parallel that fuses the commentary's womb-house with its later claim that nurture reaches teaching.

column5: father, mother, and God as partners in a child's formation
column6: The Bavli divides a child's making among father, mother, and the Holy One. Its three-agent account offers a Jewish interpretive framework for the commentary's distinction between maternal body, human caregivers, and the divine shaper.

column5: common formation in a mother's womb
column6: The speaker says that he was molded in flesh in a mother's womb and had the same entrance into life as all others. This Jewish reflection turns prenatal formation into common human kinship, echoing the commentary's one-womb logic.

column5: mother credits the Creator with her children's life
column6: The martyred brothers' mother says she does not know how they came to be in her womb and attributes life, breath, and bodily formation to the Creator. It directly combines maternal gestation with divine formative agency.

column5: remember the dangers endured in the womb
column6: Tobit tells his son to remember the many dangers his mother underwent for him in her womb. It is a close Jewish counterpart to the commentary's refusal to sentimentalize the womb-house or detach filial duty from maternal cost.

column5: honor and help a father in old age
column6: Ben Sira tells a child to help rather than grieve a father in old age. This places the grown child's mercy and practical care toward parents beside the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal of the earlier raising relationship.

column5: ordered ages for Scripture, Mishnah, commandments, and maturity
column6: Avot's age sequence makes learning and responsibility unfold in stages. It supplies a rabbinic analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as bringing a thing state by state to completion.

column5: source ر ب ب: ῥαββί glossed as Teacher
column6: John preserves the Semitic address ῥαββί and immediately glosses it as Teacher. As an actual r-b-b cognate, it substantiates the commentary's carefully developed extension from Rabb to a teacher rather than relying on the root label alone.

column5: all will be taught by God
column6: Jesus cites the promise that all will be taught by God. The direct divine-teacher formulation is a New Testament companion to the commentary's Rahman who teaches the Qur'an and teaches human expression.

column5: Jesus grows, becomes strong, and is filled with wisdom
column6: The infancy narrative describes Jesus' growth, strengthening, wisdom, and divine favor. It gives a canonical Christian rendering of child development in stages rather than a single moment of birth.

column5: Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and favor
column6: Jesus continues to advance in wisdom, stature, and favor with God and people. Its triadic maturation closely fits the commentary's movement from a child's home through cultivation toward completion.

column5: merciful as the Father is merciful
column6: Jesus grounds merciful action in the Father's mercy. This provides a father-child divine frame for the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that becomes beneficence toward others.

column5: father gives good things to children
column6: Human parents' giving of good gifts becomes the measure for the heavenly Father's generosity. It joins parental provision and divine goodness, illuminating the commentary's en'amte image of children being reared in ease.

column5: mother bird gathers young under her wings
column6: Jesus compares his desired protection of Jerusalem's children to a hen gathering her brood under her wings. The maternal protective figure supplies a New Testament meeting with the commentary's mercy, weak young, and guarded household.

column5: child placed under guardians and household managers
column6: The heir, while a child, is under guardians and managers until the father's appointed time. This is a particularly exact legal and domestic analogue for the commentary's nonbirth caregiver and the person who maintains a household's affairs.

column5: maternal labor until Christ is formed in learners
column6: Paul likens his pastoral work to being in labor until Christ is formed in his children. It turns the commentary's womb, labor, and gradual formation into an explicitly pedagogical Christian metaphor.

column5: birth pain gives way to joy at the child's arrival
column6: Jesus uses a woman in labor whose anguish turns to joy when a human being is born. It directly meets the commentary's emphasis on the bodily cost of birth, while assigning that image an eschatological meaning.

column5: teacher gives milk before solid food
column6: Paul says he gave the Corinthians milk rather than solid food because they were not ready. It is the clearest New Testament analogue to the commentary's teacher who nourishes people first with small portions of knowledge.

column5: nursing mother cherishes her own children
column6: Paul depicts his gentle pastoral care as a nursing mother cherishing her children. The image links bodily nurture and nonbiological teaching care in precisely the double register developed by the commentary.

column5: father exhorts, encourages, and comforts children
column6: Paul also compares his work to a father dealing with each child through exhortation, encouragement, and consolation. Together with maternal nursing in the preceding image, it makes cultivation a patient parental practice.

column5: growth toward mature fullness
column6: The community is to reach mature adulthood and the measure of Christ's full stature. This provides an explicit Christian endpoint for the commentary's halden hale movement to the limit of completion.

column5: bring children up in instruction of the Lord
column6: Fathers are told to bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord rather than embitter them. It directly connects household upbringing, moral formation, and teaching.

column5: newborns crave milk in order to grow
column6: Newborn infants are urged to desire pure spiritual milk so that they may grow toward salvation. The verse makes milk, infancy, teaching, and purposeful maturation one integrated image.

column5: solid food belongs to the mature
column6: Maturity is marked by solid food and trained powers of discernment. It completes the milk-to-maturity progression that the commentary's small portions of knowledge and final completion invite readers to trace.

column5: discipline yields trained righteousness
column6: Discipline is painful in the present but later yields peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it. Its temporal account of costly formation is a close conceptual partner to terbiye as gradual maturation.

column5: faithful manager supplies food at the proper time
column6: Jesus' faithful household manager gives the servants their food allowance at the proper time. This joins the commentary's qawwam-like keeper of household affairs with its secondary image of food provision and measured nurture.

column5: managing one's household and caring for God's assembly
column6: The argument reasons from managing one's own household to caring for God's church. It is a direct Christian development of the commentary's claim that standing up a household's affairs is a genuine form of care.

column5: compassion proved by material help
column6: One who sees a sibling in need and closes the inward organs of compassion is challenged to show God's love. The verse makes compassion concrete through goods and need, matching the commentary's insistence that mercy entails beneficent action.

column5: source ر ح م: brotherly compassion, רחמים
column6: Joseph's compassion for his brother is stirred so strongly that he must withdraw and weep. The Hebrew r-ḥ-m vocabulary lets the commentary's womb-derived kinship become a specific fraternal affect, without claiming that the two narratives are the same.

column5: source ق و م: Hebrew הקים, raising and establishing a descendant
column6: God promises David that he will raise up his offspring after him and establish his kingdom. Hebrew q-w-m is a real cognate field for the commentary's qawwam, but this verse shifts from daily household support to securing a child and dynasty.

column5: source ن ع م: Hebrew נעם, pleasant paths
column6: Wisdom's ways are called ways of pleasantness and her paths peace. Hebrew n-ʿ-m is cognate with the source en'amte family, but the biblical verse applies pleasantness to wisdom's path rather than importing the commentary's child-rearing sense.

column5: jealousy within a suspected marriage
column6: A husband's spirit of jealousy arises in the ordeal for a wife suspected of infidelity. It is a concrete biblical household setting for the commentary's secondary gayrah image of guarding family, but its suspicion and legal ordeal complicate any simple protective reading.

column5: returning to the mother's womb questioned
column6: Nicodemus asks whether an adult can enter a mother's womb a second time and be born. The question makes physical womb-life explicit, while the ensuing Johannine discourse redirects birth to a different, Spirit-centered register rather than the commentary's original womb-house.

column5: a chosen disciple takes Jesus' mother into his home
column6: Jesus establishes a new mother-son relation, and the disciple takes her into his own household. This is a concrete Christian scene of nonbiological family care that belongs beside the commentary's step-parent and child-minder images.

column5: God supplies an infant through the mother's breasts
column6: Augustine thanks God for providing infant food through the mother's breasts rather than treating maternal nursing as self-sufficient. This Christian reading closely parallels the commentary's distinction between the visible mother and the true divine guardian of a child's nurture.

column5: Joseph assigned as Mary's guardian
column6: In the usual chapter division, the priests assign the older Joseph to keep Mary when she can no longer remain in the temple. This infancy tradition extends the commentary's nonbirth-caregiver question into a Christian guardianship narrative; details and chapter subdivision vary by translation.

column5: virgin's womb holds the Provider as an infant
column6: Ephrem's Nativity hymn dwells on the paradox that the Provider enters the Virgin's womb and accepts infant need. It is a Syriac Christian theological rereading of womb as dwelling and nurture; stanza numbering varies across editions.

column5: painless virginal delivery in a Christian hymn
column6: The ode's birth image is commonly read as portraying the Virgin's delivery without pain. Against the commentary's laboring maternal body, it offers a specifically Christian theological reversal rather than a shared account; the ode's transmission and verse division warrant caution.
